title: Mysterious underwater ruins discovered near Mount Ararat – could be part of an ancient city
excerpt: Mysterious underwater ruins discovered near Mount Ararat – could be part of an ancient city
content:
Fun

Express newspaper

28/09/2026 22:58

Mysterious stone structures have been discovered in the deep, dark waters of Lake Van in Turkey, which some researchers believe may be part of a very ancient submerged settlement.

Divers have documented a large circular structure and a wall built of interlocking stone blocks, about 23 meters below the surface of the lake.

Researcher Matthew LaCroix, part of the team analyzing the area, says the ruins discovered so far may be only a small part of a much larger complex.

"What we know about the underwater wreckage may be just a small fragment of something much larger," he said.

LaCroix has hypothesized that the structures could be at least 11,700 years old and, based on his interpretation of the geological data, possibly as old as 40 years.

However, this date has not been confirmed by direct analysis of the stones or by archaeological excavations.

A structure that continues into the darkness of the lake

The uncovered wall contains three steps leading up to the circular structure and seven levels of stonework, which rise more than 2.4 meters from the lake bottom.

LaCroix said he measured a structure similar to a road or walkway of more than 45 meters.

"It goes on for more than 150 feet and leads you into darkness," he said.

According to him, this could mean that the structure is connected to other buildings that have not yet been discovered.

He believes that the amount of work required to build such a structure makes it impossible for it to have been created in isolation.

"There must have been a larger urban area to which this point was connected," he argued.

However, so far there is no archaeological evidence confirming the existence of a complete city under the waters of the lake.

Near Mount Ararat and the legend of Noah's Ark

The location of Lake Van also adds to the mystery.

It is located in eastern Turkey, near the border with Iran and about 145 kilometers from Mount Ararat.

Mount Ararat has long been associated with biblical traditions as the place where Noah's Ark may have ended up, although this has not been proven archaeologically.

Nearby is the Durupınar formation, which some have interpreted as a possible site of the Ark, but this idea remains debatable.

Lake Van has an area of ​​about 3,750 square kilometers and is the largest lake in Turkey.

The first discoveries began in 2017.

Turkish underwater filmmaker Tahsin Ceylan discovered the first ruins in 2017 while studying the lake's microbiome formations and characteristic fish.

He came across a stone structure resembling a fortress, next to which were circular structures with carefully crafted masonry.

A stone carved with a six-ray symbol, similar to the so-called "Flower of Life", a motif used in various cultures throughout history, was also found.

Ceylan later collaborated with LaCroix on a dive conducted in 2025.

However, the large stone wall was not noticed during the expedition itself.

He was only identified later, during the review of film footage.

How old are the ruins really?

This is also the main question that remains unanswered.

Some archaeologists have linked the structures to the Urartian period, who controlled this region about 3 years ago.

Other researchers have suggested that some parts may even be medieval and that they may have been built using older Urartian blocks.

LaCroix, however, argues that the lake's geology may point to a much earlier history.

It is known that Lake Van once had a natural outlet to the west, which was later blocked by massive eruptions of the Nemrut volcano during the Pleistocene epoch.

The Pleistocene ended around 11,700 years ago, while some estimates place major volcanic eruptions much earlier.

LaCroix argues that, if the structures were there before the water level changed, they could be much older than previously thought.

But this remains a hypothesis.

No stone taken from the ruins has been independently dated, and no archaeological excavation has been carried out to date to prove the age of the structures.

Harsh conditions make exploration problematic

Studying the area is difficult due to the characteristics of Lake Van.

The lake has no natural outlet, which causes dissolved sediments to remain in the water and greatly limit visibility.

According to LaCroix, divers typically only have a short period during the morning, approximately from 5 a.m. to 11 a.m., when conditions are suitable for exploration.

He himself has not dived to the wall, which is about 23 meters below the surface.

LaCroix said he spent only about eight minutes near the circular structure, which is located at a depth of about nine meters, while other team members filmed the surrounding areas.

"It's a perfect circle. When you dive in and look at it from above, it looks like a perfect circle," he said.

The two structures are located at a considerable distance from each other, but according to the team they are part of an underwater area mapped to about one square kilometer.

The wall was only discovered after analyzing the video

The long stone structure had not been noticed during the dive.

It wasn't until a few months later, after cameraman Brandon Barnes released footage filmed behind the circular structure, that the team realized they had documented something else.

The video appeared to show three steps leading up to the circular monument, followed by seven rows of masonry and a long structure that continued beyond.

"When I saw it, I thought, 'Oh my God, they've found something,'" LaCroix recalled.

He believes that the structure cannot simply end in nothing and that it must lead to another area.

"I still haven't been able to see where it ends. It leads somewhere. We just don't know where yet," he said.

More evidence is needed before talking about a lost city

Despite intriguing hypotheses, there is still not enough evidence to state that there is an 11,700 or 40-year-old city under Lake Van.

The dating proposed by LaCroix is ​​based on the interpretation of geological studies of volcanic eruptions and historical lake level changes, not on dating the structures themselves.

Other researchers continue to consider a Urartian or medieval origin for at least part of the ruins more likely.

LaCroix believes the lake's relatively calm waters may have helped preserve the structures.

"It's as if everything has been sitting there, preserved, waiting for humanity to discover it," he said.

Determining what this area really is will require further dives, detailed sonar mapping, and analysis by archaeologists specializing in underwater research.

Only then can it be determined whether the long structure is truly man-made, where it leads, and whether other buildings are hidden in the darkness of Lake Van. /GazetaExpress/
